summary: Describes the Magnalink Variable Resource Compression Algorithm, which allows interoperable compressors to trade off performance against available CPU and memory. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A squeezer that can work gently on weak computers and harder on strong ones, and they still understand each other.

questions: how does variable resource compression work in ppp
what is magnalink variable resource compression
how does mvrca adapt compression to available resources
what is the context identifier in mvrca
subtitle: Compression that scales with available processor and memory.

tldr.problem: Data compression is useful for PPP links, but different devices have different processing power and memory available. A single compression standard cannot work well for all of them.
tldr.mechanism: MVRCA is a compression algorithm that allows implementations to trade off compression performance against the CPU and memory resources available, while staying interoperable with other implementations.
tldr.outcome: Devices can now compress PPP traffic efficiently by selecting how hard to work, based on what they have. The algorithm is informational, not a standard.

today: RFC 1975 is Informational and describes a compression algorithm available under license. It is not a standard, and implementations that use MVRCA must obtain the full specification and licensing from Telco Systems.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Magnalink Variable Resource Compression Algorithm (MVRCA) addresses the need for PPP compression that adapts to the device using it. PPP already has a standard way to negotiate compression via the Compression Control Protocol. MVRCA defines a family of compression implementations whose performance is a function of available CPU and memory resources.

This allows each end of a PPP link to choose compression settings suited to its hardware, without compromising interoperability with the other end.
sections.plainLanguage: Different computers have different speed and memory. MVRCA lets them each pick a compression setting that fits their hardware, and they still work together.

sections.title: Compression Packets and Reliability
sections.content:
Before MVRCA compression can begin, PPP must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and the Compression Control Protocol must reach the Opened state, indicating both sides are ready.

MVRCA packets can be sent over unreliable links or, if negotiated, over reliable links as described in PPP Reliable Transmission. If frames are lost or arrive out of order, the decompressor detects this and requests resynchronization from the compressor using the CCP Reset-Request and Reset-Acknowledge messages.

Although compression can sometimes expand data, MVRCA avoids this by sending expanded packets uncompressed instead. Dictionary synchronization is maintained across both compressed and uncompressed packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Once PPP handshake is done, compression starts. If a packet gets lost, both sides know it and catch up. If a packet would get bigger when compressed, MVRCA sends it as-is instead.

sections.title: Packet Encapsulation
sections.content:
Each MVRCA packet contains a PPP Protocol Identifier, followed by a header with four fields: a Compressed flag (C) that indicates whether the data is compressed or uncompressed, a Context Identifier (CID) that selects which history buffer to use, a proprietary flag bit (E), and a Packet Integrity Byte (PIB) for detecting corruption. The compressed data follows.

The CID allows the compressor to use separate history buffers for different protocols or virtual circuits. A CID of 0 indicates packet-by-packet compression where the history buffer is cleared between packets. The Packet Integrity Byte ensures packets are compressed and decompressed correctly and that history buffer synchronization is maintained.
sections.plainLanguage: The header tells the other side: is this data squished (C flag), which dictionary to use (CID), and a checksum to spot corruption.

sections.title: Configuration and Negotiation
sections.content:
MVRCA negotiates compression settings via the Compression Control Protocol. The configuration option has type 24 and includes three parameters: FE (Features) for algorithm-specific features, History which defines the size of the compression history buffer, and Contexts which specifies how many history buffers to create (from 1 to 63).

Each context receives a history buffer of the size indicated. The P (Packet by Packet) flag enables packet-by-packet compression for context 0. When P is 1 and Contexts is 1, only packet-by-packet compression is supported with no history maintained across packet boundaries. When P is 0, packet-by-packet compression is disabled entirely.
sections.plainLanguage: Before compressing, both sides agree: how big each history buffer is, how many of them to use, and whether to squish one packet at a time or keep history across packets.

sections.title: Licensing
sections.content: Source licenses for MVRCA are available on a non-discriminatory basis. The RFC notes that implementers should contact Telco Systems Inc. (Magnalink Communications Division) for licensing evaluation and source code availability. This informational RFC does not define a standard compression algorithm in detail; implementers are responsible for obtaining the full algorithm specification and license.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm comes from a company that licenses it to anyone on fair terms. You have to get the details and permission from them.

fields.name: Compressed Flag (C)
fields.desc: 1 if data is compressed, 0 if uncompressed.

fields.name: Context ID (CID)
fields.desc: Selects which history buffer to use (0-63).
